(CNN) — For a little while, it seems that “Up,” Pixar’s 10th feature-length film, is going to be a downer.

In “Up,” Carl, a curmudgeonly senior citizen, tries to cope with the enthusiasm of Russell, a young boy. Not that there is anything wrong with an animated film tugging at our tear ducts. Still, you can sense unease rippling through the younger half of the family audience when, about five minutes into a spirited prologue, intrepid pre-pubescents Carl and Ellie abruptly become newlyweds—and then not-so-newlyweds.

They gray and stoop before our eyes, their youthful dreams of exploration exchanged for the comforts of home and domestic bliss. Ellie wants a baby but cannot have one. Their savings for the holiday of a lifetime are consumed by one rainy day and domestic disaster after another, until there is no lifetime left—not for Ellie, anyway.

That leaves us with Carl, a grumpy homebody voiced by Ed Asner, who makes WALL-E look like a chatterbox. And he is one of the main characters. No, I did not hear anyone asking when the dancing penguins were going to appear, but I would wager someone was thinking it.

Watch a preview of “Up” »

Such misgivings are unfounded. When it comes to razzmatazz, “Up” delivers the goods. Not penguins, precisely, but far more than the airborne house promised in the commercials.

There is a mythical, multicolored bird that may or may not be a snipe, answers to the name Kevin, and displays a fondness for candy bars. There are zeppelins, old-time explorers, and talking dogs—a whole pack of them, in fact. Dogs that serve wine, play cards, and fly biplanes.

And there is Russell, a chubby Boy Scout—or “Wilderness Explorer”—who appears on Carl’s doorstep when he least expects it. After all, Carl wants to be free, and to achieve that freedom, he launches his house into the sky with thousands of balloons. How was he to know Russell was nearby?

“Up” does not always soar. The dogs’ canine high jinks are closer to “Beverly Hills Chihuahua” than one would expect from Pixar, which generally does not play so fast and loose with the laws of nature merely for a few cheap laughs. But if the muttering mutts keep the children happy, well and good.

The film is on surer ground as it develops the relationship between Carl and Russell while they float high above the Earth. Russell is all wide-eyed innocence and boundless enthusiasm, haplessly helpful. He is the mirror image of the child Carl once was, if only the old man were capable of recognizing it.

But rather than looking around him, Carl remains focused on placing his cherished home in the prime location he mistakes for his ultimate destination: the lost world of Paradise Falls. The image of Carl valiantly dragging his house through jungles and over mountains will resonate with anyone paying off a mortgage.

iReport.com: Share your review of “Up”

Written by Bob Petersen and directed by Petersen and Pete Docter—both Pixar veterans—“Up” blends allegory, adventure, and sheer imaginative exuberance. The balance is not quite as precise as in Pixar’s best films, but its lightness is appealing, and Russell, voiced by Jordan Nagai, is an irresistible character. At just 8 years old, he is already carrying emotional baggage of his own, but he is all heart—the kind of child who gives children a good name.

Screening in 3-D where possible, “Up” does not go overboard with stereoscopic gimmickry, though it does exploit depth of field in a series of exhilarating cliffhangers and dogfights.

Funny, poignant, and full of life, “Up” easily ranks among the best films of the year so far. See it with someone you care about.

“Up” is rated PG and runs 96 minutes.

(CNN) — For its opening stretch, Pixar’s 10th full-length movie, “Up,” seems as though it may be headed in a decidedly gloomy direction.

The story centers on Carl, an irritable elderly man who must contend with the relentless energy of a young boy named Russell. There is nothing inherently wrong with an animated movie aiming for an emotional response, but younger audience members may grow uneasy during the film’s lively opening sequence. Within roughly five minutes, the adventurous children Carl and Ellie become newlyweds and then rapidly age. Their hair turns gray, their bodies bend, and their childhood ambitions of exploring the world give way to domestic happiness and the security of home.

Ellie hopes to have a child but learns that she cannot. Meanwhile, the couple repeatedly dips into the money saved for their dream vacation, using it to cover one emergency and household setback after another. Eventually, Ellie runs out of time before they can take the trip.

Carl is left behind: a grouchy, reclusive man voiced by Ed Asner who is so quiet that he makes WALL-E seem talkative. And Carl is one of the movie’s central figures. Nobody in the theater actually asked when the dancing penguins would arrive, but it is easy to imagine the thought crossing someone’s mind. Watch a preview of “Up” ».

Those concerns, however, prove unnecessary. When it comes to spectacle, “Up” provides plenty. It does not offer penguins, exactly, but it delivers much more than the balloon-lifted house shown in advertisements. The adventure includes Kevin, a legendary, brightly colored bird that may or may not be a snipe and has a fondness for candy bars. There are also zeppelins, explorers from an earlier era, and an entire group of talking dogs. These dogs pour wine, play cards, and pilot biplanes.

Then there is Russell, a plump Boy Scout—or, as the movie calls him, a “Wilderness Explorer”—who appears at Carl’s home at the most inconvenient possible moment. Carl wants freedom, so he sends his house soaring into the air with thousands of balloons. He has no idea Russell is nearby when he takes off.

“Up” does not succeed at every turn. The dogs’ comic antics feel more like something from “Beverly Hills Chihuahua” than the kind of humor typically associated with Pixar. The studio usually avoids casually ignoring the rules of nature simply to generate easy laughs. Still, if the grumbling, speaking dogs entertain children, they serve their purpose.

The film is much more confident when exploring Carl and Russell’s developing bond as they travel high above the ground. Russell is innocent, endlessly excited, and well-meaning, though his efforts to help often go wrong. He resembles the boy Carl once was, even if Carl cannot see the similarity.

Rather than paying attention to the person beside him, Carl remains determined to place his treasured house in what he believes is its perfect setting and his final destination: the lost world of Paradise Falls. Anyone making mortgage payments may identify with the sight of Carl struggling to pull his house through jungles and across mountains.

iReport.com: Share your review of “Up”

The screenplay was written by Bob Petersen, and the film was directed by Petersen and Pete Docter, both longtime Pixar contributors. “Up” combines symbolism, action, broad comedy, and uninhibited imagination. Its various elements are not blended quite as smoothly as they are in Pixar’s finest films, but the movie’s buoyant quality remains charming. Russell, voiced by Jordan Nagai, is especially difficult to resist. Although he is only 8, he already carries emotional burdens of his own. Even so, he is generous and sincere—the sort of child who improves the reputation of children everywhere.

Where available, the movie is presented in 3-D. It avoids excessive reliance on stereoscopic tricks, instead using visual depth effectively during a series of exciting near-falls and aerial battles.

Humorous, moving, energetic, and alive, “Up” deserves to be counted among the year’s best films to date. See it with someone important to you.

Pixar’s *Up* begins on a surprisingly somber and emotionally mature note. Through a largely wordless montage, the film follows Carl and Ellie as they grow old together, endure the heartbreak of infertility, and repeatedly postpone their dream of traveling to Paradise Falls. Their life is loving but ordinary, shaped by unexpected expenses and missed opportunities. Before they can finally make the journey, Ellie dies, leaving Carl alone with their memories and unrealized plans.

Voiced by Ed Asner, Carl becomes a grumpy, withdrawn widower who clings to the house he shared with Ellie. Although he initially seems like an unlikely hero for an animated adventure, his grief, stubbornness, and lingering devotion make him one of the film’s most compelling central characters.

Despite this deeply emotional opening, *Up* soon transforms into a colorful and imaginative adventure. Carl attaches thousands of balloons to his house and lifts it into the sky, setting out for South America. The journey introduces flying houses, enormous zeppelins, legendary explorers, dramatic landscapes, and other spectacular elements that give the film a playful sense of wonder.

Carl does not make the trip alone. He is unexpectedly joined by Russell, an enthusiastic young Wilderness Explorer who happened to be on the porch when the house took flight. Cheerful, talkative, and determined to earn his final merit badge by assisting the elderly, Russell serves as an energetic contrast to Carl’s irritable solitude.

The adventure becomes even stranger with the appearance of Kevin, a rare, mythical-looking bird covered in brilliant multicolored plumage. Carl and Russell also encounter a pack of dogs equipped with collars that translate their thoughts into speech. These dogs not only talk but also carry out elaborate, human-like tasks, adding both comedy and absurdity to the film’s mix of heartfelt drama and extravagant adventure.

Pixar’s *Up* begins in a way few family films would dare. After a lively introduction to Carl Fredricksen and Ellie, two children united by their fascination with adventure, the film quietly follows their life together. They marry, restore an old house, and dream of traveling to Paradise Falls in South America. Yet ordinary expenses and disappointments repeatedly force them to postpone the journey. In a nearly wordless montage, their shared ambitions give way to the realities of aging, and Ellie eventually dies before they can fulfill their dream. The sequence is tender, economical, and devastating, capturing an entire marriage in only a few minutes.

That somber opening initially seems like a risky foundation for an animated adventure aimed partly at children. Carl is not a conventional hero: he is elderly, stubborn, lonely, and increasingly cut off from the changing world around him. Facing removal from the home he shared with Ellie, he decides to escape. By attaching thousands of balloons to the house, he sends it floating into the sky and sets off for Paradise Falls, determined to place it where Ellie always imagined they would live.

Carl soon discovers that he has an accidental passenger. Russell, an earnest and relentlessly cheerful young Wilderness Explorer, was standing on the porch when the house took flight. He needs one final badge for assisting an elderly person, although Carl has little interest in being assisted. Their contrasting personalities provide much of the film’s comedy: Russell is talkative, trusting, and enthusiastic, while Carl is irritable and reluctant to form any new attachment.

Once they reach South America, the film becomes a more conventional adventure, though it never entirely abandons the emotional weight of its opening. Carl and Russell encounter Kevin, an enormous and brilliantly colored flightless bird, as well as Dug, a friendly dog whose special collar translates his thoughts into speech. Dug belongs to a pack of talking dogs controlled by Charles Muntz, the famous explorer Carl and Ellie idolized as children. Now consumed by his desire to prove the existence of Kevin’s species, Muntz has become a dangerous and obsessive figure.

The dogs supply both action and broad comedy. Their translated thoughts capture recognizable canine impulses: they become distracted by squirrels, obsess over food, and compete for dominance. Some of this humor is deliberately childish, and the film occasionally relies too heavily on easy jokes about animal behavior. Yet the silliness also prevents the story from becoming overwhelmed by its darker concerns. Dug’s uncomplicated affection is particularly effective, gradually breaking through Carl’s defensive isolation.

Visually, *Up* is filled with imaginative spectacle. The image of a small house drifting beneath a vast canopy of multicolored balloons is instantly memorable, combining whimsy with a persistent sense of fragility. The South American landscape offers cliffs, waterfalls, mist, and strange wildlife, while the airborne house becomes both a vehicle and a symbol. Carl drags it behind him as if he were carrying his past, and the film makes that burden increasingly literal. His devotion to Ellie’s memory has kept him moving toward their old dream, but it has also prevented him from recognizing the new relationships forming around him.

This is where *Up* proves more thoughtful than its adventure plot might suggest. Carl initially believes that honoring Ellie means completing their plan exactly as they imagined it. Gradually, however, he learns that their life together was not merely a prelude to the journey they never took. Their marriage—with all its ordinary pleasures, setbacks, and compromises—was itself the great adventure. Letting go of the house does not mean forgetting Ellie; it means accepting that love can remain meaningful without becoming a prison.

Russell’s story deepens this idea. Beneath his comic enthusiasm is a child who longs for attention from an absent father. Carl, who begins the film determined to avoid human contact, slowly becomes the dependable adult Russell needs. Their bond gives both characters a second chance at family. Carl cannot recover the future he once expected, but he can still participate in life, care for others, and discover new forms of happiness.

There may have been concern that children would resist a film centered on an aging widower, grief, and unfulfilled dreams. *Up* answers that concern by refusing to separate emotional seriousness from entertainment. It offers chases, aerial battles, exotic creatures, talking dogs, and slapstick comedy, but it also trusts younger viewers to understand loneliness, change, and loss. Not every joke rises to the level of the film’s best moments, and the villain-driven climax is less original than the opening. Even so, the adventure remains connected to Carl’s emotional transformation.

*Up* ultimately demonstrates what animation can accomplish when it is treated not as a genre but as a medium. Its bright colors and extravagant fantasy appeal to children, while its reflections on marriage, mortality, regret, and renewal speak powerfully to adults. The film is funny and exciting, but its lasting impact comes from its conviction that life continues after disappointment—and that the adventures we overlook may be as important as the ones we spend years hoping to begin.

**Review: Pixar’s ‘Up’ soars on heart, humor and adventure**

Pixar’s *Up* begins with what may be one of the most emotionally powerful sequences ever placed in an animated family film. In a nearly wordless montage, audiences watch Carl Fredricksen meet, marry and grow old with his childhood sweetheart, Ellie. Their shared dreams, quiet joys and painful disappointments unfold in minutes, giving the colorful adventure that follows an unexpectedly profound foundation.

Now a lonely, stubborn widower, Carl—voiced with gruff warmth by Ed Asner—ties thousands of balloons to his house and sets off for South America, hoping to fulfill Ellie’s lifelong dream. But he soon discovers an accidental passenger: Russell, an enthusiastic young Wilderness Explorer whose nonstop optimism clashes neatly with Carl’s impatience.

The pair is joined by Kevin, a giant exotic bird, and Dug, a lovable dog whose high-tech collar translates his thoughts into speech. Dug provides some of the movie’s best laughs, particularly when his canine focus is instantly derailed by the possibility of a squirrel. The humor works for children without talking down to adults, balancing slapstick with sharp character comedy.

The journey eventually becomes a fast-moving adventure involving a legendary explorer, a pack of talking dogs and action sequences staged high above a dramatic jungle landscape. Some of the villain-driven plot feels more conventional than the opening, but director Pete Docter keeps the story grounded in Carl’s emotional transformation.

The 3-D effects add depth to the sweeping cliffs, floating balloons and aerial chases without overwhelming the story. Rather than relying on objects flying toward the audience, the technology expands the film’s sense of space and wonder.

Visually inventive, consistently funny and deeply moving, *Up* demonstrates Pixar’s unusual ability to combine sophisticated themes with broad entertainment. Its opening may break your heart, but the film ultimately lifts the spirit.

**Verdict:** A beautifully crafted adventure that ranks among Pixar’s finest.

**Pixar’s *Up* is a touching, adventurous family film—but it earns that description by taking children’s emotions seriously rather than avoiding sadness.**

Its famous opening compresses a lifetime of love, disappointment, and loss into a largely wordless sequence. Themes of infertility, aging, bereavement, and letting go will resonate most strongly with adults, while younger children may simply understand that Carl has lost someone he loved. The melancholy continues through Carl’s loneliness and stubborn attachment to the past, so sensitive children may need reassurance.

That emotional weight is balanced by a bright, increasingly playful adventure: a floating house carried by balloons, an enthusiastic young Wilderness Explorer, a colorful giant bird, talking dogs, slapstick chases, and an airborne climax. Dug, the distractible dog, supplies especially reliable comedy. There is also plenty of movement and visual invention to hold children’s attention after the subdued opening.

The danger can be intense for very young viewers. Characters face falls, fire, aggressive dogs, and a threatening villain, though the violence remains stylized and largely bloodless.

Overall, *Up* successfully balances mature themes with humor, color, and action. It is an excellent choice for most school-age children and adults, offering different rewards to each. Preschoolers may enjoy the animals and spectacle, but particularly sensitive ones could find the opening loss and later peril upsetting.

### ‘Up’ Sends Pixar Soaring, Even When Its Story Loses Altitude

Pixar’s tenth feature-length film, **“Up,”** begins with a love story of extraordinary economy and emotional force. In a nearly wordless montage, shy Carl Fredricksen and spirited Ellie grow from childhood friends into an elderly married couple, sharing a dream of visiting **Paradise Falls**. Their life does not unfold as planned, and Ellie’s death leaves Carl alone with a house full of memories. The sequence is among the studio’s finest achievements: tender without becoming mawkish, and honest about disappointment as well as devotion.

The main adventure is more fanciful. Carl, threatened with removal to a retirement home, attaches thousands of balloons to his house and floats toward South America. He soon discovers an accidental passenger: **Russell**, an overeager Wilderness Explorer hoping to earn his final merit badge. Once near Paradise Falls, they encounter **Kevin**, a brilliantly colored, flightless bird, along with a pack of **talking dogs** whose collars translate their thoughts into speech.

Director Pete Docter handles this collision of grief and slapstick with remarkable confidence. The dogs—especially the guileless Dug—provide some of the film’s broadest laughs, though their comic antics and the ensuing action occasionally make the second half feel more conventional than the haunting opening promises. A climactic villain plot involving disgraced explorer Charles Muntz is exciting but less original than the domestic emotions that set the story in motion.

The voice performances give the film its warmth. **Ed Asner** makes Carl’s gruffness funny while preserving the sorrow beneath it; every complaint sounds like armor against further loss. **Jordan Nagai** brings Russell an appealing mixture of chatter, insecurity and stubborn kindness. **Christopher Plummer** lends Muntz polished menace, while **Bob Peterson**, as Dug, turns canine simplicity into irresistible comedy. Kevin needs no dialogue to emerge as one of the picture’s liveliest personalities.

“Up” is not perfectly balanced: its emotional realism and cartoon spectacle sometimes seem to belong to different films. Yet its central insight remains clear and affecting. Paradise Falls may be the destination, but Carl’s real journey is away from preserving the past and toward risking affection again. Few family movies aim so high; fewer still reach such moving heights.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a detailed, mostly positive review of “Up” that compares it with other animated movies, evaluates the Carl–Russell relationship and 3-D presentation, and ends with the rating and runtime.
counterfactuals.output:
Pixar’s *Up* is an adventurous, funny, and unexpectedly moving animated film that demonstrates how effectively the studio can blend emotional sophistication with broad family entertainment. Its premise—a widower lifting his house into the sky with thousands of balloons—suggests a whimsical fantasy, but the movie is grounded in recognizable feelings of love, grief, loneliness, and the difficulty of moving forward.

The opening sequence, which traces the shared life of Carl Fredricksen and his wife, Ellie, is among Pixar’s finest achievements. With minimal dialogue, it compresses decades of affection, disappointment, and ordinary happiness into a few minutes. Like the best passages in *WALL-E*, it trusts music, images, and gesture rather than constant explanation. This emotional foundation gives Carl’s later adventure real weight: His journey to Paradise Falls is not simply a comic escape but an attempt to fulfill an old promise and preserve his connection to Ellie.

Carl is an unusual animated protagonist. He is elderly, stubborn, physically limited, and initially more interested in avoiding people than helping them. His square, compact design mirrors his defensive personality, while the rounded, energetic Russell seems built to disrupt Carl’s carefully maintained isolation. Russell, a young Wilderness Explorer who accidentally becomes a passenger on the flying house, could easily have been an irritating sidekick. Instead, his enthusiasm and vulnerability make him essential to the story.

The Carl–Russell relationship is the film’s emotional center. Their early exchanges are driven by impatience: Carl sees Russell as an inconvenience, while Russell is too eager and inexperienced to recognize Carl’s need for solitude. Gradually, however, their shared ordeal reveals what each lacks. Russell needs an attentive adult who will value his efforts and simply spend time with him; Carl needs a new human connection that does not erase his love for Ellie but allows that love to lead him back into life. Their bond becomes a surrogate grandfather-grandson relationship without feeling mechanically imposed. Small moments—Carl helping Russell across difficult terrain or quietly listening to him discuss his absent father—are often more affecting than the movie’s large action scenes.

In this respect, *Up* compares favorably with other animated films built around mismatched partnerships, such as *Shrek*, *Ice Age*, and Pixar’s own *Finding Nemo*. Those films also pair a reluctant, emotionally guarded character with a more talkative companion, but *Up* gives the formula additional poignancy by connecting it to bereavement and aging. Carl’s change of heart is not merely a lesson in teamwork; it is an acknowledgment that honoring the past does not require withdrawing from the present.

The supporting characters provide the film’s more conventional comedy. Dug, a dog whose collar translates his thoughts into speech, is an inspired comic creation precisely because his dialogue captures the uncomplicated, distractible mind of a friendly pet. Kevin, the enormous exotic bird pursued by explorer Charles Muntz, adds color and physical humor. Muntz himself is less nuanced than Carl or Russell, and the movie becomes somewhat less distinctive once it shifts toward aerial combat, chases, and a familiar villainous confrontation. Compared with the sustained thematic focus of *Ratatouille* or the near-wordless elegance of *WALL-E*, *Up* occasionally feels as though two movies have been joined together: an intimate drama about loss and a hectic jungle adventure.

Even so, the action is inventive and visually coherent. The floating house is one of modern animation’s most memorable images, with its dense canopy of brightly colored balloons contrasting against Carl’s dark clothes and boxy silhouette. Paradise Falls, inspired by the dramatic landscapes of South America, has a scale and beauty that make the journey feel genuinely mythic.

The 3-D presentation is restrained and effective. Rather than continually throwing objects toward the audience, the filmmakers use depth to emphasize distance, height, and atmosphere. The house drifting through clouds, the vast drop beside Paradise Falls, and the aerial climax gain spatial clarity without turning the film into a theme-park demonstration. The effect is immersive rather than aggressive. Viewers watching in 2-D will not lose the story’s essential impact, but 3-D enhances the contrast between Carl’s formerly confined existence and the enormous world he finally enters.

*Up* may not be Pixar’s most perfectly structured film, but its emotional ambition, visual imagination, and beautifully developed central relationship outweigh its more routine villain and action elements. It belongs near the studio’s strongest work and stands apart from many animated adventures by treating childhood and old age with equal sympathy. It is a film about keeping promises, releasing burdens, and realizing that life’s most meaningful adventures may be the relationships that arrive unexpectedly.

**Rating: PG. Runtime: 96 minutes.**
